# **The PGM Jewellery Monitor** _Covering activity in the Chinese platinum and palladium jewellery manufacturing industry from July to October 2011_ _December 2011_ **David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** **07 December 2011** ##### **New York:** - A strong gold price has not deterred Chinese consumers from buying gold jewellery and this market continues to grow. Platinum jewellery has not suffered from this growth and demand in this market looks set to grow this year too. Palladium jewellery demand is still shrinking within China. • The fall in the platinum price below that of gold has allowed manufacturers and retailers to maintain and even build margins. However, at a retail level, platinum is not being sold below the price of gold jewellery and the consumer response to the unexpected price differential between the two materials has been minimal. In fact, a falling platinum price may have been slightly negative for retail sales compared to previous expectations for the past few months. • The outlook for the platinum market in the next few months is positive with retailers expected to start building stocks imminently ahead of the Chinese New Year buying season. The separation of Chinese New Year and Valentine’s Day should provide two separate buying seasons next year and add to demand. • The use of recycled platinum by jewellers in China increased from July to October compared to the previous four month period. However, the recent spell of lower metal prices has seen the use of this recycled material decrease. • The palladium jewellery market continues to shrink. The sharp increase in the metal price in late 2010 discouraged consumers from buying palladium jewellery and encouraged the industry to recycle stocks of old, unsold pieces. Recycling rates have risen and manufacturing output continues to soften with net demand for new palladium from this industry falling as a result. 200 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10166 0130 Tel: +1 212 878 4122 ##### **London:** 4th Floor, St Martins Court, 10 Paternoster Row, London EC4M 7BB Tel: +44 20 7489 6767 ##### **Hong Kong:** Suite 1306, Two Exchange Square, 8 Connaught Place, Central, Hong Kong Tel: +852 2899 2026 ##### **Tokyo:** 2-1 Ohtemachi 1-Chome, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo 100 Tel: +81 33 285 3407 ##### **Singapore:** 80 Robinson Road, #15-02, Singapore, 068898 Tel: +65 6372 8050 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | The PGM Jewellery Monitor** **07 December 2011** ## **Platinum** Manufacturing volumes Forecast volumes Optimism Pt:Pd ratio

Chinese platinum jewellery manufacturing grew in July to Octo

ber compared to the previous four month period, despite strong competition from a buoyant gold jewellery market. Sales of platinum during the key Golden Week/National Day holidays were healthy but not too remarkable, with an increase in the weight of metal sold of perhaps five per cent compared to the previous year. Jewellery factory output was also higher than in the previous few months, a little better than had been expected, while stock levels have remained stable, although credit remains hard to obtain. Any easing of credit availability could allow manufacturers to add to working stocks next year, boosting demand for platinum. Year-to-date sales of platinum are therefore better than they were at the same point in 2010. At a retail level, platinum is _NEVER_ seen at a lower price than gold and most customers remain unaware that gold has moved into a premium over platinum. If this premium is maintained over an extended period, this situation may change. However, in the short term, platinum’s lower metal price has had no impact on consumer behaviour. On the contrary, consumers within China tend to buy precious metal jewellery in periods of rising prices and the recent decline in the platinum price has depressed sales in the last few weeks. _High figures indicate an increase in a measure and low figures indicate a decrease in a measure. 5 indicates no change from the last reporting period. Pt:Pd ratio compares the amount of each metal used by manufacturers with a high figure showing platinum taking market share from palladium._ The industry remains optimistic about demand, particularly if the platinum price stabilises or starts to rise. The upcoming Chinese New Year (CNY, in mid-January) means that retailers will soon start to rebuild stocks. The greater separation between CNY and Valentine’s Day will effectively create two separate buying periods and will enhance consumer buying. Margins and profitability have improved compared to the previous four month period and also compared to a year earlier with stronger demand and a robust approach to pricing at the factories largely responsible. However, wage inflation and the availability of trained personnel remain problematic. These will keep pressure on the manufacturers in financial terms and are likely to deter new entrants companies from entering this sector. The use of recycled platinum rose slightly compared to March-June 2011 period. However, this has slowed since September with lower platinum prices discouraging consumers from selling or trading in old pieces. We expect the use of recycled metal to fall from 2010 levels, meaning that net demand should increase at a faster rate than gross demand. 2

The long, steady decline in manufacturing and retail volumes of palladium jewellery within China continued in the four months from July to October 2011. Manufacturing volumes were roughly 15-20 per cent lower than a year earlier although they were some 10 per cent stronger than in the previous four month period. Relatively few companies are now producing palladium jewellery with some now only producing pieces to order. With only this small number of manufacturers still active in this market, there has been little pressure on margins which are essentially unchanged in recent months. Despite falling demand, there therefore seems little prospect of further companies exiting the palladium jewellery market in the short term. _High figures indicate an increase in a measure and low figures indicate a decrease in a measure. 5 indicates no change from the last reporting period._ The outlook for the next few months is more positive as the lower palladium price has made jewellery made from this metal more cost-competitive. More importantly, the forthcoming Chinese New Year and Valentine’s Day sales seasons should encourage more buying by retailers and wholesalers to build stocks. There has been little if any change to manufacturers’ stocks of palladium, whether inprocess materials or finished goods. The decrease in the size of this market means that an increasing proportion of business is manufacturing to order (instead of manufacturing for stocks which are sold to retailer purchasing managers visiting Shenzhen). There is little scope now for further reductions in stocks of finished palladium pieces but, as demand dwindles, we would expect to see a slow decrease in working stocks of metal. A major change is an increase of between ten and twenty per cent in the amount of recycled palladium being used by the industry from July to October compared to the previous four month period (the latest Johnson Matthey figures suggest over a hundred per cent increase in the use of recycled palladium this year). High metal prices (compared to last year) have driven retailers and wholesalers to recycle and remanufacture old stock and an increasing proportion of manufacturing is from cannibalisation of this old, unsold stock. The recent price fall may decrease the industry’s desire to recycle this material. In any case, as this market shrinks in size, the amount of metal available for recycling will shrink. We do not expect the recent fall in the price of palladium to reignite consumer demand. 3

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | The PGM Jewellery Monitor** **07 December 2011** ## **Notes to methodology** This survey uses similar methodology to previous reports issued by Mitsui Precious Metals on the gold refining market. Mitsui surveys a large number of participants in the Chinese jewellery market to obtain semi-quantitative information on the market. This data is then weighted by the importance of the respondent and averaged across the industry. High figures indicate an increase in the measure and low figures indicate a decrease in a measure. 5 indicates no change from the last reporting period. The survey does not aim to report on changes in consumer behaviour except in an anecdotal sense but rather to add some further detail to the qualitative understanding of demand for metal at the major jewellery manufacturers within China. For quantitative figures on demand, we refer the reader to the usual Johnson Matthey and GFMS reports on the platinum group metal market. ## **Timescale** This survey covers manufacturing and other activity from July to October 2011 inclusive, a period wh

ich includes the October National Day holidays. Forward-looking production forecasts relate to the next four month period while optimism measures longer term views. Backward-looking data is compared to the same period one year earlier. ## **Terminology** In any report on a technical subject, the use of technical terms is unavoidable so we list here definitions of as many of these terms as possible: |950, 990, 999|95%, 99% or 99.9% pure alloy
